document.title: Comments of the Solar Energy Industries Association in response to PJM Interconnection, L.L.C.’s Reliability Backstop Procurement proposal

pages.text:
UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
BEFORE THE
FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION 
PJM Interconnection, L.L.C. 
) 
) 
)
Docket No. ER26-3380-000
COMMENTS OF THE SOLAR ENERGY INDUSTRIES ASSOCIATION 
Pursuant to Rule 213 of the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission’s (“Commission”) 
Rules of Practice and Procedure,1 the Solar Energy Industries Association (“SEIA”)2 hereby 
submits these comments in response to PJM Interconnection, L.L.C.’s (“PJM”) filing proposing a 
Reliability Backstop Procurement (“RBP Proposal”). PJM filed the RBP Proposal pursuant to 
Section 205 of the Federal Power Act (“FPA”),3 proposing revisions to the PJM Open Access 
Transmission Tariff (“Tariff”) and the Reliability Assurance Agreement Among Load Serving 
Entities (“RAA”) to establish a one-time procurement mechanism to address resource adequacy 
shortfalls in the PJM Region.4 As set forth below, SEIA does not oppose the RBP Proposal and 
submits these comments to identify targeted areas where the Commission and PJM may wish to 
consider refinements that could further unlock capacity participation and reduce procurement 
costs. 
1 18 C.F.R. § 385.213 (2026). 
2 SEIA is the national trade association of the solar energy industry. As the voice of the industry, SEIA works to 
support solar as it becomes a mainstream and significant energy source by expanding markets, reducing costs, 
increasing reliability, removing market barriers, and providing education on the benefits of solar energy. The 
comments contained in this filing represent the position of SEIA as a trade organization on behalf of the solar industry, 
but do not necessarily reflect the views of any particular member with respect to any issue. 
3 16 U.S.C. § 824d (2024). 
4 Capitalized terms not defined herein have the same meaning as in the PJM Tariff, RAA or the RBP Proposal, as 
applicable.

2 
I.
INTRODUCTION
SEIA does not oppose PJM’s RBP Proposal as a necessary and timely response to the 
resource adequacy challenges facing the PJM Region. The recent Base Residual Auctions 
(“BRAs”) for the 2027/2028 and 2028/2029 Delivery Years each cleared 5.6% below the PJM 
Region Installed Reserve Margin of 20%,5 driven primarily by unprecedented additions of large 
loads—particularly data centers—that have outpaced supply additions. PJM’s proposal to conduct 
a one-time backstop procurement to secure approximately 6,831.3 MW of Unforced Capacity 
(“UCAP”) is a reasonable mechanism to address this shortfall, particularly given the immense 
pressure from states, governors, and the White House for PJM to act expeditiously.6
Indeed, the RBP Proposal represents a measured approach to address a serious reliability 
concern. PJM has designed the procurement initiative to balance urgency with market principles—
including a pay-as-bid structure,7 a bilateral contracting offset mechanism,8 and a Contract for 
Difference (“CfD”) settlement approach that mitigates ratepayer costs. While SEIA commends 
PJM for bringing this proposal forward under extraordinary time constraints, SEIA respectfully 
offers the following comments to identify areas where the Commission and PJM may wish to 
consider refinements that could further unlock capacity participation and reduce procurement 
costs—both in connection with the RBP and, where applicable, in the broader capacity market 
reforms that PJM and the Commission may undertake in subsequent proceedings. 
5 See RBP Proposal at 124 (explaining that the 2027/2028 and 2028/2029 Base Residual Auctions each cleared 5.6% 
below the PJM Region Installed Reserve Margin of 20%). 
6 See Statement of Principles Regarding PJM, National Energy Dominance Council, 1 (Jan. 16, 2026), available at: 
https://www.energy.gov/documents/statement-principles-regarding-pjm (“NEDC/PJM Governors’ Principles”) 
(calling for a backstop auction no later than September 2026). 
7 See RBP Proposal at 65–67 (proposing a pay-as-bid clearing structure for the RBP). 
8 See id. at 35–42 (describing the Qualifying RBP Offset UCAP MW mechanism by which bilateral contracts reduce 
the procurement target).

3 
II.
COMMENTS 
A.
ELCC Uncertainty and Commercial Operation Date Requirements May 
Limit Timely Capacity Participation. 
The RBP Proposal requires successful resources to commit to a fixed period of 15 Delivery 
Years beginning with the 2028/2029 Delivery Year9 and to achieve commercial operation 
(“COD”) by no later than June 1, 2032. While SEIA does not oppose the 15-year term or the COD 
requirement, it identifies two concerns with how these parameters interact with existing capacity 
market rules in ways that may limit participation and increase procurement costs.  
First, there is a temporal mismatch: the RBP is designed to address a shortfall beginning in 
the 2028/2029 Delivery Year, yet resources are not required to achieve COD until June 1, 2032. 
SEIA notes that PJM’s proposed clearing structure10 partially addresses this concern by ranking 
offers first by the earliest Delivery Year in which capacity would be available and then by least 
cost—thereby prioritizing resources that can deliver capacity sooner. However, the COD deadline 
itself warrants further attention, as discussed below.11
Second, the 15-year commitment exposes resources to long-duration ELCC variability that 
is difficult or impossible for an individual resource to underwrite—a challenge that exists 
independent of PJM’s clearing structure and that may deter participation from resources that could 
otherwise contribute to meeting the reliability need. 
While PJM captures ELCC decline in its published 10-year forecast, PJM has not published 
a forecast out to 15 years.12 An individual RBP resource cannot control, predict, or hedge its ELCC 
9 See RBP Proposal at 34. 
10 See Proposed Tariff, Attachment DD, section 18.5(f)(ii) (providing that RBP Sell Offers shall be selected “in rank 
order from earliest to latest offered Delivery Year, and then in least-cost order based on the levelized cost ($/MW-
day) of UCAP MW over the fixed 15-year term, until the Final RBP Target is satisfied”). 
11 See id. at 39. 
12 See PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., Preliminary ELCC Class Ratings for Period 2026/2027 Through 2034/2035, 
available 
at: 
https://www.pjm.com/-/media/DotCom/planning/res-adeq/elcc/preliminary-elcc-class-ratings-for-
period-2026-2027-through-2034-2035.ashx.

4 
accreditation 10 to 15 years into the future. The result is that rational developers will either embed 
a disproportionate risk premium in their bids or decline to participate.13 SEIA supports the concept 
of a fixed-for-floating ELCC mechanism—whereby a resource’s RBP contract volume would be 
set based on PJM’s published ELCC forecast at the time of commitment, while year-over-year 
variance between the forecast and actual ELCC flows into RPM settlement, where such variability 
already manifests annually for all resources. This approach would decouple the developer’s long-
term revenue certainty from uncontrollable ELCC fluctuations, yielding lower, more competitive 
bid prices.14
Turning to the COD requirement, the June 1, 2032 deadline is too late to address the 
immediate shortfall PJM faces. The 2028/2029 BRA cleared 6,831.3 MW short of the PJM Region 
Reliability Requirement.15 PJM should not have to wait four years for generation to come online. 
Solar, energy storage, and demand response resources—which have the shortest construction 
timelines of any asset class—are the marginal resources of capacity during this period and can 
deliver timely UCAP. At the same time, because PJM’s transmission expansion planning process 
addresses deliverability needs reactively—identifying and constructing network upgrades only 
after capacity has been committed—larger resources that require significant network upgrades to 
become deliverable may not achieve full deliverability by June 1, 2032. This is particularly true 
given documented network upgrade construction timelines of three to five years or more in the 
13See REV Renewables, LS Power, Middle River Power & Geronimo Power, PJM Reliability Backstop Procurement 
Design — Executive Summary, at 2 (June 30, 2026), available at: https://www.pjm.com/-/media/DotCom/committees-
groups/cifp-rbp/2026/20260630/20260630-item-02k---rev-renewables--ls-power---mrp---geronimo---rbp---
executive-summary.pdf. 
14See id. (explaining that an individual RBP resource cannot control, predict, or hedge its ELCC accreditation 10 to 
15 years into the future, and that unhedgeable long-duration ELCC uncertainty will command a risk premium above 
expected loss); see also MN8 Energy, Feedback on Select RBP Design Components, at 3 (June 11, 2026), available 
at: https://www.pjm.com/-/media/DotCom/committees-groups/cifp-rbp/2026/20260611/20260611-item-04d---mn8-
energy-presentation.pdf (proposing a fixed-for-floating class ELCC mechanism and noting that today’s project 
financing environment necessitates conservative views on capacity attributes, which is reflected in higher bid prices). 
15 See RBP Proposal at 7.

5 
PJM region. PJM itself publicly acknowledged in a January 2026 stakeholder meeting that 
significant new capacity additions are unlikely to come online before 2032 due to, among other 
factors, transmission constraints.16 While the COD requirement cannot account for all real-world 
issues,17 this limitation should be considered in evaluating the effectiveness of the RBP. SEIA 
therefore urges PJM to prioritize timely UCAP and to ensure that resources capable of delivering 
capacity sooner are appropriately valued. 
In light of these challenges, SEIA encourages the Commission and PJM to provide greater 
capacity certainty to all resources to maximize participation in the RBP. This includes stability in 
ELCC accreditation values and broader capacity market reforms that would give prospective 
participants confidence in projecting their obligations and revenues over the commitment period. 
The RFI administered by Charles River Associates identified over 100 GW of prospective supply 
interested in participating;18 ensuring that market rules support—rather than discourage—this 
participation is essential to achieving the lowest possible procurement costs for ratepayers. 
Accordingly, SEIA recommends that PJM and the Commission address ELCC accreditation 
uncertainty and prioritize timely UCAP delivery—both of which would expand the pool of 
competitive offers and reduce procurement costs for ratepayers. 
16 See Devin Leith-Yessian, Government-Proposed “Backstop” Auction to Test PJM Stakeholder Process, RTO
INSIDER (Jan. 26, 2026), available at: https://www.rtoinsider.com/124178-government-proposed-backstop-auction-
test-pjm-stakeholder-process/ (“Even with a backstop auction, [David] Mills [PJM board chair and interim CEO] said 
there are significant barriers to getting new resources built, including transmission upgrades, financing, tariffs, siting, 
permitting and supply chain constraints. Significant new capacity is unlikely to be available until 2032.”). 
17 See PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 195 FERC ¶ 61,197, at P 43 (2026); see also PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 190 
FERC ¶ 61,084, at P 157 (2025). 
18 See RBP Proposal at 68 (noting the RFI administered by Charles River Associates identified over 100 GW of 
prospective supply interested in participating); see also PJM Reliability Backstop RFI Summary, Charles River 
Associates, at 5 (May 27, 2026), available at: https://www.pjm.com/-/media/DotCom/committees-groups/cifp-
rbp/2026/20260527/20260527-informational-only---reliability-backstop-rfi-summary---charles-river-associates.pdf
(reporting 397 potential supply-side projects by 87 entities, representing approximately 136 GW in total potential 
capacity).

6 
B.
The Compressed Timeline for Bilateral Contracting May Result in Higher 
Procurement Costs. 
The compressed timeline for the RBP procurement window may limit bilateral contracting 
opportunities and result in unnecessarily higher auction clearing prices. While SEIA does not 
oppose the RBP Proposal in principle, it notes that without sufficient time for load-serving entities 
and prospective suppliers to negotiate bilateral contracts, the Qualifying RBP Offset mechanism 
may not achieve its intended effect of reducing the procurement target. PJM is targeting 
commencement of the procurement window on September 30, 2026, with a three-week offer 
submission window and clearing concluding six weeks thereafter.19
Indeed, the RBP Proposal appropriately incorporates a mechanism by which bilateral 
contracts and self-supply arrangements for new capacity serving new load reduce the Initial RBP 
Target through the Qualifying RBP Offset. In theory, this mechanism should exert downward 
pressure on auction prices by reducing the quantity of capacity that must be procured through the 
competitive auction process.20 However, SEIA is concerned that the accelerated timeline from 
PJM Board approval on July 27, 2026, to the anticipated September 30, 2026 procurement 
commencement may not provide sufficient opportunity for load-serving entities and prospective 
suppliers to negotiate and execute the bilateral contracts that would qualify as offsets. In turn, if 
the time available for bilateral contracting proves insufficient, fewer Qualifying RBP Offsets may 
be available to reduce the Final RBP Target, and the resulting auction may clear a larger volume 
of capacity at potentially higher prices than would otherwise be necessary. SEIA encourages the 
Commission and PJM to monitor the effectiveness of the bilateral contracting mechanism and to 
19 See id. at 32, 48 (describing the offer submission window of three weeks, with clearing and selection concluding 
six weeks thereafter). 
20 See id.

7 
consider adjustments if the compressed timeline proves insufficient to support meaningful bilateral 
engagement. 
SEIA recognizes that PJM and the Commission are under immense pressure—including 
from the thirteen PJM-state governors and the National Energy Dominance Council, whose joint 
statement of principles21 urged expeditious action—for this procurement to proceed on an 
expedited basis, and that the fundamental timeline is unlikely to change. SEIA is lodging this 
concern into the record insofar as the current RBP may set precedent for future central 
procurements. 
C.
Recommendations for Unlocking Additional Capacity 
In order to enable PJM to unlock additional capacity and reduce procurement costs, SEIA 
respectfully offers the following recommendations for the Commission’s and PJM’s consideration: 
First, PJM should offer a fixed-for-floating ELCC swap option for resources 
participating in the RBP and for bilateral arrangements qualifying as RBP Offsets. Year-over-
year volatility in ELCC accreditation values creates significant uncertainty for resources 
contemplating long-term commitments such as those required by the RBP. Stabilizing ELCC 
values—whether through longer averaging periods22 or other mechanisms—would give 
prospective participants greater confidence in projecting their capacity revenues over the 15-year 
commitment period and would thereby encourage broader participation. When a resource can 
reasonably forecast its accredited capacity value over the commitment term, it can underwrite 
financing and commit to a 15-year obligation with confidence that its revenues will support the 
investment. Absent such predictability, resources face the risk that declining ELCC values will 
21 See NEDC/PJM Governors’ Principles at 1. 
22 Cf. PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 186 FERC ¶ 61,080 (2024) (accepting PJM’s transition from average to marginal 
ELCC methodology, reflecting the Commission’s ongoing consideration of ELCC approaches that balance accuracy 
with predictability).

8 
erode their revenue stream below the level needed to service project debt, deterring participation 
in the RBP altogether.
Second, the Commission should consider whether the minimum contract length for 
bilateral arrangements under the RBP is sufficient to enable meaningful bilateral contracting.23
The minimum five-year contract requirement for bilateral arrangements24 qualifying as RBP 
Offsets may be insufficient to enable meaningful bilateral contracting. While parties are free to 
negotiate contracts of any length, the five-year minimum effectively sets a floor that, as a practical 
matter, is likely to define the standard term for bilateral arrangements under the RBP Proposal. 
Project economics and financing structures for new capacity resources typically require a 
commitment term closer to ten years to justify the capital investment and development risk 
associated with new generation. To the extent the Commission can encourage bilateral contracting 
by providing clarity that longer-term bilateral arrangements are acceptable and supported under 
the Qualifying RBP Offset framework, such action would incentivize supply participation in 
bilateral contracting and thereby reduce reliance on the auction, with attendant downward pressure 
on clearing prices.
Third, moving beyond the RBP, PJM and the Commission should pursue seasonal 
capacity markets.25 A seasonal market construct would better align capacity obligations with the 
periods in which resources can deliver capacity value, recognizing that different resource types 
contribute to reliability in different seasons. Seasonal markets would enable a broader array of 
23 See Proposed Tariff, Attachment DD, section 18.2(c)(i). 
24 Proposed Tariff, Attachment DD, section 18.2(c)(i); see also RBP Proposal at 39–40 (explaining that bilateral 
contracts must have a minimum term of at least five Delivery Years to qualify as Qualifying RBP Offset UCAP MW). 
25 See PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 186 FERC ¶ 61,080, at P 293 (2024) (encouraging PJM to continue evaluating 
whether and how a seasonal capacity construct could support reliability and efficiency); see also Transmittal Letter of 
PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., Docket No. ER24-99-000, at 18 (Oct. 13, 2023) (stating that “PJM and its stakeholders 
are committed to continuing to assess the design of PJM’s capacity construct, including whether and how a seasonal 
capacity market could help support reliability and efficiency in the PJM region”).

9 
resources to participate in meeting PJM’s reliability needs, including resources whose 
contributions are concentrated in particular seasons. Because ELCCs depend heavily on the 
balance of reliability risk between seasons, seasonal capacity markets should also reduce ELCC 
volatility, improving the hedging value of resources and making them easier to underwrite.26 This 
reform would complement the RBP by expanding the pool of resources willing and able to make 
long-term capacity commitments. 
Fourth, PJM and the Commission should address the commercial barriers that prevent 
surplus interconnection service from delivering additional accredited capacity to the system.
PJM’s surplus interconnection service allows new resources to use interconnection rights at 
existing points of interconnection, providing a pathway for developers to add capacity to existing 
renewable sites with minimal network upgrades and through an expedited interconnection 
process.27 The Commission recently accepted PJM’s proposed tariff revisions in Docket No. 
ER25-778-000 to remove engineering barriers that previously blocked surplus interconnection 
requests—including the elimination of the “materiality” review that effectively denied most 
surplus requests before any study could be performed.28 However, significant commercial barriers 
remain that prevent surplus interconnection from delivering its full potential. 
Under the current framework, surplus resources face a potentially unworkable choice. 
Because PJM’s Tariff only grants capacity interconnection rights (“CIRs”) and ELCC 
26 See Comments of MN8 Energy, PJM CIFP – Large Load Additions Stakeholder Process, at 22 (Nov. 19, 2025), 
available 
at: 
https://www.pjm.com/-/media/DotCom/committees-groups/cifp-lla/2025/20251119/20251119-
stakeholder-written-comments.pdf (discussing capacity market reforms needed for a developer to enter into medium- 
to long-term contracts). 
27 See PJM Tariff, Part VIII, Subpart E, § 414 (Surplus Interconnection Service). 
28 See PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 190 FERC ¶ 61,083, at PP 30, 33 (2025) (accepting PJM’s proposed tariff 
revisions to remove eligibility restrictions on surplus interconnection service and facilitate the rapid expansion of 
generating facilities on PJM’s system); see also Comments of the Clean Energy Associations, Docket No. ER25-778-
000, at 1–3 (Jan. 13, 2025) (“Clean Energy Associations Surplus Comments”) (urging Commission acceptance of 
PJM’s surplus interconnection reforms as a pathway to unlock GWs of storage capacity).

10 
accreditation to surplus resources that merge with the existing facility as a single hybrid resource,29
a developer seeking capacity value through surplus interconnection must elect hybrid treatment—
which potentially requires unwinding existing power purchase agreements, tax equity structures, 
and lender arrangements. The alternative—interconnecting independently as a co-located 
resource—preserves independent financing but limits the surplus resource to energy-only market 
participation, forfeiting capacity value entirely. Because hybrid treatment requires combined 
market participation as a single resource,30 it does not allow for component-level settlement, and 
capacity performance penalty risk cannot be isolated from the host resource. Lenders to the 
existing facility will rarely consent to the addition of a surplus resource under these conditions, 
because it exposes the existing project to performance liability arising from a resource it does not 
own or control. This effectively renders the surplus interconnection pathway commercially 
unavailable for many projects, regardless of whether the interconnection path is clear. 
To address these barriers and unlock the significant capacity potential of surplus 
interconnection, SEIA recommends three reforms. First, PJM should enable surplus resources to 
obtain independently recognized and bankable capacity positions—distinct from the host 
resource—without requiring the wholesale restructuring of existing commercial arrangements. 
This could be achieved through several mechanisms, including: (i) split UCAP settlement between 
component accounts; or (ii) CIR transfer mechanisms between co-located resources.31 Whichever 
29 See PJM Tariff, Part VIII, Subpart E, § 414 (Surplus Interconnection Service); see also Hybrid Resources Market 
Model Selection—Problem Statement, PJM Interconnection, L.L.C. (Aug. 2026) (“Hybrid PS/IC”), available at: 
https://www.pjm.com/-/media/DotCom/committees-groups/committees/mic/2026/20260805/20260805-item-04-1---
hybrid-resources-market-model-selection---problem-statement.pdf (recognizing that under current rules, the only 
pathway for surplus resources to obtain capacity value is to become a hybrid resource with the existing project). 
30 See Hybrid PS/IC (discussing issues relating to hybrid resource combined market participation as a single market 
unit in PJM’s energy, capacity, and ancillary services markets). 
31 Under PJM’s current framework, a surplus interconnection arrangement results in a revised or amended Generation 
Interconnection Agreement for the existing facility, rather than a separate, standalone GIA for the surplus resource. 
See PJM Tariff, Part VIII, Subpart E, § 414(B)(2) (providing that a “revised Interconnection Service Agreement or 
Generation Interconnection Agreement will be prepared and issued to the owner of the existing or planned Generating

11 
mechanism is adopted, the objective should be to provide each component of a surplus 
arrangement with independent settlement, revenue allocation, and penalty isolation necessary to 
support separate financing.  
Second, whether adopted in connection with the foregoing reforms or as a standalone 
measure, PJM should establish clear protections ensuring that a default or performance issue 
arising from the surplus resource cannot create cross-default risk or otherwise interfere with the 
existing resource’s GIA or operations. This protection is essential to obtaining lender consent: 
absent an explicit structural separation of liability, lenders to the existing facility will not approve 
the addition of a surplus resource that could jeopardize the project’s existing financing and 
operational arrangements.  
Third, SEIA encourages PJM to evaluate whether additional resources or process 
modifications can be devoted to surplus interconnection studies to reduce the time from application 
to completion, particularly for projects that could deliver capacity within the RBP’s timeframe. 
The Commission’s acceptance of PJM’s Docket No. ER25-778-000 reforms removed the prior 
automatic disqualifications that blocked surplus requests, but developers now need timely study 
completion to bring resources online within the timeframes contemplated by the RBP.32 Together, 
these reforms—addressing commercial structure, lender protections, and study timelines for 
surplus interconnection—would enable surplus interconnection to serve as a meaningful near-term 
pathway for delivering additional accredited capacity to the PJM system, potentially unlocking 
Facility”). This structure means the surplus resource’s market participation, obligations, and potential liabilities are 
housed within the existing project’s agreement, creating the cross-default risk discussed above. 
32 See PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 190 FERC ¶ 61,083 at PP 30, 33–34 (accepting revisions that expand availability 
of surplus interconnection service and noting that PJM’s proposal “should expand the use of surplus interconnection 
service and allow additional capacity resources to connect to the PJM system”); see also Clean Energy Associations 
Surplus Comments at 3 & n.10.

12 
gigawatts of storage and other resources that are positioned to connect quickly at existing points 
of interconnection.33
These reforms are not prerequisites for Commission acceptance of the RBP Proposal, but 
rather constructive improvements that would enhance the effectiveness of the procurement and 
address resource adequacy challenges on a forward-going basis. Moreover, while SEIA raises 
these concerns in the context of the RBP, the principles underlying these recommendations—
including the need for predictable capacity accreditation, sufficient time for bilateral contracting, 
and workable commercial frameworks for surplus interconnection—are not limited to this 
proceeding and warrant the Commission’s attention as it considers broader capacity market 
reforms. Indeed, the NEDC and PJM Governors’ Principles—which, as the RBP Proposal 
acknowledges, inform the design and objectives of the RBP—contemplate a subsequent “return to 
market fundamentals” and continued refinement of PJM’s capacity market framework,34 and these 
recommendations are consistent with that ongoing effort. 
III.
CONCLUSION
For the foregoing reasons, SEIA respectfully submits that while the RBP Proposal 
represents a necessary and timely response to PJM’s resource adequacy challenges, the 
Commission should consider the refinements identified herein—including accommodations for 
bilateral contracting timelines, measures to provide capacity certainty over the commitment term, 
removal of commercial barriers to surplus interconnection, and reforms to unlock additional 
participation—as it evaluates the RBP Proposal as a means of securing the timely addition of new 
capacity. To the extent the Commission identifies opportunities to incorporate such improvements, 
33 See Clean Energy Associations Surplus Comments at 3. 
34 See NEDC/PJM Governors’ Principles at 1 (urging PJM to “embark on a stakeholder process to reform the capacity 
market to ensure long-term viability and prevent consumers from bearing excessive ongoing costs”); see also RBP 
Proposal at 6–8 (citing and implementing the NEDC/PJM Governors’ Principles).

13 
whether in its order on the RBP Proposal or in subsequent proceedings, doing so would further the 
shared objective of procuring sufficient capacity at the lowest reasonable cost. SEIA supports 
PJM’s effort to address the resource adequacy shortfall on an expedited basis and appreciates the 
opportunity to provide these comments. 
Respectfully submitted, 
Melissa Alfano
